subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: giving in to every relative's demand [Pitfall]
passage:
Eshaan and I only wanted a small evening. Then an aunt asked for a second function, an uncle for forty more guests, a cousin for a live band. Each time we said okay, because that was easier than a fight. The budget doubled. By the week of the wedding I looked at the decoration list and couldn't recognise us in any of it. We snapped at each other over the seating plan. Eshaan said, "Whose wedding is this?" and I had no answer. Looking back, I'd say yes to fewer things, and say a kind, early no to the first one.

Saurabh

qa.q: What did the aunt ask for?
qa.a: The aunt asked for a second function.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when asking whose wedding it was?
qa.a: Eshaan was frustrated and hurt, feeling the wedding no longer belonged to the couple.

qa.q: What could the couple have done at the first request, and why?
qa.a: They could have given a kind, early no to the second function, because a small refusal at the start is easier than many concessions later.

qa.q: How might the relatives have seen the couple's yeses?
qa.a: The relatives probably thought the couple was happy to add things, since nobody said otherwise, and did not see the strain building.

grounding: Illustrates giving in to every relative's demand about guests, events and rituals, so the budget doubles, the wedding feels no longer the couple's and stress strains the relationship.

passage:
Pre-marriage counsellor's note — sessions with Akash and Sunaina, Jaipur

When they first came in, in January, the plan was a two-day wedding for two hundred. By their fourth session in March, it had become four days and six hundred.
Akash described it without much feeling. His mausi wanted a sangeet. Sunaina's bua wanted a separate mehendi. An elder uncle insisted on a special havan with priests from Varanasi. Each time, they said yes to avoid hurt feelings. His friend Rafiq, who was handling the bookings, had told them the budget had roughly doubled.
In session, Sunaina said quietly, "It doesn't feel like our wedding anymore." Akash didn't answer. They had not had dinner together in two weeks, they said, because every evening was spent on calls with relatives.
What I did next: I suggested they each write the three things that matter most to them, and bring the lists next week.

qa.q: How many guests were on the plan by March?
What did Sunaina mean by "It doesn't feel like our wedding anymore"?
qa.a: Sunaina felt sad and disconnected, as if relatives' wishes had taken over the event the couple wanted.

qa.q: What else could Akash and Sunaina have done when the first extra request came?
qa.a: They could have agreed their own shared priorities first and used them to say a kind no, instead of saying yes to every relative.

qa.q: How is Rafiq affected by the couple giving in to every demand?
qa.a: Rafiq, handling the bookings, watches the budget roughly double and has to deliver the bad news, which puts Rafiq in an uncomfortable spot.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a couple adding guests, events and costly rituals to please relatives until the budget doubles and stress strains them.

Friday, 1 a.m.

Can't sleep again. Rohit and I had our worst fight yet, about napkins. Napkins!
It isn't really about napkins. It started in October with a simple plan: one day, close family, the garden behind Rohit's parents' house. Then his Dadi wanted a proper sangeet. Then my Chachi wanted a cocktail night "for the younger ones". Then someone said a wedding without a horse would look cheap. Every time, we said yes, because saying no to elders felt rude.
Now it's three events, a horse, a DJ, and a budget that is double what we started with. Rohit's working weekends to cover it.
Noor asked me today, "Are you excited?" I didn't know what to say.
I used to daydream about this wedding. Now I just want it to be over.
— Preeti

qa.q: Where was the wedding originally going to be held?
qa.a: In the garden behind Rohit's parents' house.

qa.q: How does Preeti feel about the wedding now?
qa.a: Preeti feels drained and unhappy, unable to answer whether it is exciting and just wanting it to be over.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Preeti and Rohit handled relatives' requests?
qa.a: Agree together on a few non-negotiables and check each new request against them, saying no kindly when it doesn't fit.

qa.q: What might Noor notice when Preeti can't answer the question?
qa.a: Noor may sense that Preeti is stressed and unhappy, and might worry about how the planning is affecting Preeti and Rohit.

grounding: It shows a couple saying yes to every relative's request so the budget doubles, the event stops feeling like theirs, and stress strains their relationship.
